skills.name: clarity-checker
skills.title: Clarity checker
skills.summary: Checks a draft before you send it and lists anything a reader could misread, miss or find stressful.
skills.what_it_does: Paste in a draft and ask "is this clear?" or "how will this come across?". You get a one-line verdict, then a short list of issues, each quoting your words with a suggested fix, so you can tidy it up in your own voice. It looks for the things neurodivergent readers often find hard, such as hidden asks, vague deadlines, a "quick chat" with no reason, idioms and long paragraphs, and these make messages clearer for everyone. If your draft is already clear, it says so and doesn't invent problems.
how_it_works: You paste your draft and ask whether it is clear, or how it will come across.
It gives a verdict: clear, mostly clear, or needs work.
It lists up to ten issues, most important first, each with the words it means and a short fix.
It checks how clearly the message reads, not whether the facts are right, but it will mention a date that doesn't match its weekday.
If you want the whole thing rewritten, ask and the Clear message rewriter takes over.
good_for: A last check before an email goes to a whole cohort or team
Checking the tone of a message you're worried about
Getting feedback while keeping your own wording
Working out what a confusing email you received is asking
not_for: Rewriting the message (use the Clear message rewriter)
try_saying: How will this come across to a student?
Check the tone of this, I don't want it to sound harsh.
Would someone who reads things literally understand this?

skills.name: clear-message-rewriter
skills.title: Clear message rewriter
skills.summary: Rewrites an email, announcement or set of instructions so it is clear, direct and easy to act on.
skills.what_it_does: Paste in a draft and ask for it to be clearer. You get a rewrite that says what the message is about in the first line, numbers each thing you are asking for, and swaps vague timing like "ASAP" for a real date. If your draft doesn't give the date, it marks it [date to confirm] instead of guessing. It is designed with neurodivergent readers in mind, which makes messages clearer for everyone. You can ask for a style, such as direct and literal, structured, short, predictable or gentle on tone. You don't need to say anything about the reader's health or diagnosis, and it works better if you don't.
how_it_works: You paste your draft and, if you like, say who it's for or how they like to receive information.
It puts the purpose first, numbers the asks and replaces idioms with plain wording, keeping your level of formality.
For a meeting request, it makes sure the reader knows why, when, where, how long and whether to prepare, and asks you to fill in anything missing.
It keeps every fact, date and requirement, and keeps optional things optional.
It ends with a short list of what it changed and anything you need to decide before you send it.
good_for: Emails asking colleagues or students to do something by a date
"Can we have a chat?" messages that might worry the reader
Students writing to a tutor, for example to ask for an extension
not_for: Policies, regulations, assessment briefs or formal case letters (it offers a plain cover note instead)
Making a message more formal or professional
Translation, or prompts for AI tools
try_saying: Can you make this email clearer?
My colleague prefers direct, literal messages. Can you redo this one?
Rewrite this so it doesn't worry the student.
Restructure this announcement so nobody misses the deadline.

skills.name: meeting-minutes
skills.title: Meeting minutes and actions
skills.summary: Turns meeting notes or a transcript into formal minutes, action notes or a decisions log, with a clear list of actions, owners and dates.
skills.what_it_does: Paste in your notes, a Teams transcript or a meeting recap and ask for minutes. You get a draft in the right style: formal minutes for committees and boards, short action notes for team meetings, or a one-line-per-decision log. It never guesses. Anything unclear, such as a vague owner, a figure given two ways or a date like "next Friday", is marked [to confirm] and listed so you can check it with the chair before you send anything out.
how_it_works: You paste or upload your notes or transcript and say what you need, for example "write up the minutes".
It picks the format from the kind of meeting and tells you which one it used.
It records only what was actually agreed, and leaves out side conversations and small talk.
If the notes include personal details, such as a named student's circumstances or a colleague's sickness, it leaves them out and tells you what it removed.
It ends with a numbered list of actions (owner and due date) and a list of points to check with the chair, to delete before you circulate.
good_for: Committee, board and panel minutes from rough notes
Turning a Teams transcript into a tidy record
Pulling out just the decisions from a project board
not_for: Agendas or meeting invites (it won't write minutes for a meeting that hasn't happened)
Appeal, misconduct, disciplinary or grievance hearings
Summarising an email thread or a document
try_saying: Can you write up minutes from these notes?
Turn this Teams transcript into formal minutes for the School Board.
Just give me a decisions log from this project board.
Who agreed to do what? Make me an action list with owners and dates.

coming_soon.title: Catch me up
coming_soon.summary: Summarises a long email thread or set of documents into what happened, what's decided and what you need to do.

coming_soon.title: Workshop plan reviewer
coming_soon.summary: Reviews a staff workshop or training plan as a critical friend, with a short list of prioritised fixes.
